answer:
Pick **Idea B**, with strict commercial milestones. Your four years inside a utility give you an advantage in understanding workflows, data and credible repair decisions. A’s friendly letters of intent and tentative investor interest are weak evidence of demand. Its competitors demonstrate a market, but you haven’t identified why customers would switch to you.

B’s biggest danger is exhausting your savings before procurement finishes. Domain knowledge helps you build; it doesn’t establish willingness or ability to pay.

- **Month 1:** Interview 15–20 utilities, including operators, budget owners and procurement staff. Identify an upcoming repair-planning decision, available data, budget, council dates and payment timing. Seek two pilot candidates with named sponsors and documented approval steps. Investigate engineering firms as potential paying distribution partners, without assuming they bypass municipal approvals.
- **Months 2–3:** Deliver one narrow output: an explainable pipe-priority list and repair-budget report using existing records. Handle onboarding manually. Compare predictions against simple age/material rules and operator judgments using historical data withheld from development. Sparse failure records may support useful planning without supporting precise failure forecasts. You own customer work; your cofounder owns implementation.
- **Months 4–6:** Target two paid pilots, including one outside your existing relationships, and one conversion to an ongoing contract. Measure planning time saved, influence on repair decisions, onboarding effort and achievable annual pricing. Six months cannot reliably establish avoided failures.

Assume no investment arrives. Recalculate runway including both founders and business expenses, and protect a personal reserve.

Reassess at month three if no lawful purchase route fits your runway. Continue beyond month six only with demonstrated value and repeatable sales economics; otherwise change B’s buyer or scope, or stop before exhausting your savings.
